Prior-odds threshold for the Probability of Direction pd

Source: R/pd.adjust.R
pd.adjust.Rd

Converts an upper bound, set by the researcher, on the prior probability of the sign opposite to the claimed one into the threshold that pd must exceed before a direction is claimed. The function accepts either a vector of pre-computed pd values or a matrix of posterior draws, from which pd values are computed internally. Both direction-agnostic and directional tests are supported: the direction argument controls how pd is computed per hypothesis. The threshold is governed by \(\pi_0\) (argument pi0), the upper bound on the prior probability that a parameter lies on the side of null.value opposite to the claimed one (or equals null.value). Equivalently, one may supply \(\Pr(H_0)\) (argument p0), the largest prior probability that no claim in the family is correct, from which \(\pi_0 = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}\) is recovered if the parameters are independent a priori. For each hypothesis the function also reports pd.adj, the posterior probability of the claimed direction (favoured or predicted) under the prior in the class most skeptical of it; under the same prior the other side has probability 1 - pd.adj, so the two sum to one. A direction is claimed when pd.adj exceeds \(c\), which is the same as \(pd > c^*\).

Usage

pd.adjust(
  pd = NULL,
  draws = NULL,
  p0 = NULL,
  pi0 = NULL,
  null.value = 0,
  direction = NULL,
  order = FALSE,
  threshold = 0.975,
  alpha = NULL
)

Arguments

pd

Numeric vector of direction-agnostic pd values in \([0.5, 1]\). With pd input every test is treated as direction-agnostic and direction is ignored; for directional tests, supply draws. Ignored if draws is supplied.

draws

Optional matrix or data frame of posterior draws (columns = parameters). If provided, pd values are computed automatically from the draws according to direction and null.value.

p0

Numeric scalar in \((0, 1)\). The largest prior probability that no directional claim in the family is correct (\(\Pr(H_0)\)). Supply either pi0 or p0, not both. When p0 is given, \(\pi_0\) is derived, for parameters independent a priori, as \(\pi_0 = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}\).

pi0

Numeric scalar in \((0, 1)\). An upper bound, set by the researcher, on the prior probability that a parameter lies on the side of null.value opposite to the claimed one (or equals null.value). Because the same pi0 is applied to every test, it is also an upper bound on the expected proportion of parameters in the family that are not on the claimed side, null effects included, so a judgment about how many null effects the family could contain can guide its choice. Values below 0.5 are set to 0.5, with a warning, so that no penalty is applied. Supply either pi0 or p0, not both.

null.value

Numeric scalar or vector. The null (reference) value against which the posterior is evaluated, specified on the scale of the posterior. A single scalar applies the same null to all parameters; a vector of length ncol(draws) assigns a distinct null to each parameter. Ignored when pd is supplied directly. Defaults to 0. The class of priors behind the threshold is defined for a within-model prior symmetric about the null value (see Details), which holds for flat priors and for priors centred on it.

direction

Character vector of "greater", "less", or "two.sided" (or NULL). Specifies the testing mode for each hypothesis: "greater" for a positive directional test (\(\Pr(\theta > \theta_\text{null})\)), "less" for a negative directional test (\(\Pr(\theta < \theta_\text{null})\)), and "two.sided" for direction-agnostic testing (maximum over both sides). A scalar is recycled to match the number of parameters; a mixed vector allows different modes across hypotheses. Defaults to NULL (direction-agnostic for all parameters).

order

Logical. If TRUE, the returned rows are ordered by decreasing pd (strongest directional evidence first). If FALSE (the default), rows are returned in input order, so the output stays aligned with the columns of draws (or the elements of pd).

threshold

Numeric scalar in \((0.5, 1)\). The threshold \(c\) on pd without penalty (default 0.975, a two-sided per-test \(\alpha = 0.05\)). The function reports the threshold implied by \(c\) and pi0, \(c^* = c\,\pi_0 / ((1-\pi_0)(1-c) + c\,\pi_0)\).

alpha

Optional numeric scalar in \((0, 1)\). A convenience parameterization of threshold on the error scale: when supplied, the two-sided cutoff is set to \(c = 1 - \alpha/2\) (so alpha = 0.05 gives threshold = 0.975), overriding any threshold value.

Value

An object of class pd_adjust (a data.frame with a dedicated print.pd_adjust method), with one row per hypothesis. Columns: pd (the probability of direction, to be compared with threshold.adj), pd.adj (the posterior probability of the claimed direction under the prior in the class most skeptical of it, to be compared with threshold), pi0, m, and direction. When order = TRUE the rows are sorted by decreasing pd. When draws are supplied, the output additionally includes median.est (posterior median per parameter) and null.value. The print method shows \(m\), \(\pi_0\), the thresholds \(c\) and \(c^*\), and the columns that are constant across rows (null.value, direction) in a header, followed by the per-test table; all columns remain available for programmatic access. The object also carries, as attributes, the threshold threshold (\(c\)), the adjusted threshold threshold.adj (\(c^*\)), the corresponding two-sided per-test Type I error rates alpha.nominal (\(2(1-c)\)) and alpha.eff (\(2(1-c^*)\)); retrieve them with, e.g., attr(x, "threshold.adj"). The threshold threshold.adj is an exact function of \(c\) and \(\pi_0\), but the reported per-test rate alpha.eff uses the identity \(\alpha = 2(1 - c)\), which holds only when the null pd is approximately uniform on \([0.5, 1]\).

Details

Following Jeffreys (1938) and Westfall et al. (1997), the prior odds of each directional claim in the family are penalized. With pi0 the penalty is the same for any number of tests; with p0, \(\pi_0 = \Pr(H_0)^{1/m}\) and the penalty grows with the number of tests. Because the direction of a claim is chosen by the data, the penalty is applied over a class of priors: the within-model prior is reweighted on the two sides of null.value, so that the prior probability of each direction lies between \(1-\pi_0\) and \(\pi_0\), and a claim is made only if its posterior probability exceeds \(c\) under every prior in the class. For parameters with independent posteriors, this is equivalent to $$pd > c^*, \qquad c^* = \frac{c\,\pi_0}{(1-c)(1-\pi_0) + c\,\pi_0},$$ and the function reports \(c^*\) (threshold.adj). The smallest posterior probability is reached under the prior that gives the claimed direction probability \(1 - \pi_0\); under that prior the posterior probability of the claimed direction is $$pd_{adj} = \frac{pd\,(1-\pi_0)}{pd\,(1-\pi_0) + (1-pd)\,\pi_0},$$ reported as pd.adj, and \(pd_{adj} > c\) if and only if \(pd > c^*\). With correlated posteriors, the bound over the class can be stricter than this rule. The posterior used for estimation is not modified. The class is defined for a within-model prior that is symmetric about null.value, as are priors centred on it and, as a limit, flat priors.

Direction-agnostic tests ("two.sided"): pd is \(\max\!\big(\Pr(\theta > \theta_\text{null} \mid y),\, \Pr(\theta < \theta_\text{null} \mid y)\big)\) on \([0.5, 1]\), and a claim is made in the favoured direction when \(pd > c^*\).

Directional tests ("greater" or "less"): pd is the posterior mass on the predicted side, on \([0, 1]\), and the predicted direction is claimed when \(pd > c^*\).

Mixed use of directional and direction-agnostic tests within the same call is supported: each element of direction is handled independently, and the same threshold \(c^*\) applies to all hypotheses regardless of their directionality.

References

Berger, J. O. (1994). An overview of robust Bayesian analysis. Test, 3(1), 5–124. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02562676

Westfall, P. H., Johnson, W. O., & Utts, J. M. (1997). A Bayesian perspective on the Bonferroni adjustment. Biometrika, 84(2), 419–427. https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/84.2.419

Jeffreys, H. (1938). Significance tests when several degrees of freedom arise simultaneously. Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A. Mathematical and Physical Sciences, 165(921), 161–198. https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1938.0052

Storey, J. D. (2003). The positive false discovery rate: A Bayesian interpretation and the q-value. The Annals of Statistics, 31(6), 2013–2035. https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1074290335

Scott, J. G., & Berger, J. O. (2006). An exploration of aspects of Bayesian multiple testing. Journal of Statistical Planning and Inference, 136(7), 2144–2162. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jspi.2005.08.031

Scott, J. G., & Berger, J. O. (2010). Bayes and empirical-Bayes multiplicity adjustment in the variable- selection problem. The Annals of Statistics, 38(5), 2587–2619. https://doi.org/10.1214/10-AOS792

Examples

# From a vector of pd values
pd_values <- c(H1 = 0.999, H2 = 0.946, H3 = 0.813, H4 = 0.763,
H5 = 0.891, H6 = 0.987)
pd.adjust(pd = pd_values, p0 = 0.4)
#> Prior-odds threshold for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi0 = 0.8584
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9958
#>   direction = two.sided
#> 
#>       pd pd.adj
#> H1 0.999 0.9940
#> H2 0.946 0.7430
#> H3 0.813 0.4177
#> H4 0.763 0.3469
#> H5 0.891 0.5742
#> H6 0.987 0.9261
#> 
#> pd.adj: Pr(claimed direction | y) under the prior in the class most skeptical
#>         of it; 1 - pd.adj is the probability of the other side under that prior.
#> Claim a direction when pd.adj > 0.975, or equivalently pd > 0.9958.

# Equivalent call specifying pi0 directly
pd.adjust(pd = pd_values, pi0 = 0.4^(1/6))
#> Prior-odds threshold for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi0 = 0.8584
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9958
#>   direction = two.sided
#> 
#>       pd pd.adj
#> H1 0.999 0.9940
#> H2 0.946 0.7430
#> H3 0.813 0.4177
#> H4 0.763 0.3469
#> H5 0.891 0.5742
#> H6 0.987 0.9261
#> 
#> pd.adj: Pr(claimed direction | y) under the prior in the class most skeptical
#>         of it; 1 - pd.adj is the probability of the other side under that prior.
#> Claim a direction when pd.adj > 0.975, or equivalently pd > 0.9958.

# Simulate draws
Sigma <- matrix(0, nrow = 6, ncol = 6); diag(Sigma) <- 1
mu    <- c(1, -0.1, 0.8, 0, 2, 3)
draws <- MASS::mvrnorm(n = 4000, mu = mu, Sigma = Sigma)
colnames(draws) <- c("H1", "H2", "H3", "H4", "H5", "H6")

# From posterior draws
pd.adjust(draws = draws, pi0 = 0.7, null.value = 0)
#> Prior-odds threshold for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi0 = 0.7
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9891
#>   null value = 0, direction = two.sided
#> 
#>    median.est     pd pd.adj
#> H1     0.9860 0.8358 0.6856
#> H2    -0.1175 0.5350 0.3302
#> H3     0.7761 0.7822 0.6062
#> H4    -0.0089 0.5030 0.3025
#> H5     1.9500 0.9762 0.9463
#> H6     2.9866 0.9995 0.9988
#> 
#> pd.adj: Pr(claimed direction | y) under the prior in the class most skeptical
#>         of it; 1 - pd.adj is the probability of the other side under that prior.
#> Claim a direction when pd.adj > 0.975, or equivalently pd > 0.9891.

# Order the rows by strength of evidence
pd.adjust(draws = draws, pi0 = 0.7, null.value = 0, order = TRUE)
#> Prior-odds threshold for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi0 = 0.7
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9891
#>   null value = 0, direction = two.sided
#> 
#>    median.est     pd pd.adj
#> H6     2.9866 0.9995 0.9988
#> H5     1.9500 0.9762 0.9463
#> H1     0.9860 0.8358 0.6856
#> H3     0.7761 0.7822 0.6062
#> H2    -0.1175 0.5350 0.3302
#> H4    -0.0089 0.5030 0.3025
#> 
#> pd.adj: Pr(claimed direction | y) under the prior in the class most skeptical
#>         of it; 1 - pd.adj is the probability of the other side under that prior.
#> Claim a direction when pd.adj > 0.975, or equivalently pd > 0.9891.

# Mix of directional and agnostic tests with parameter-specific nulls
pd.adjust(draws = draws, pi0 = 0.6, null.value = c(0.2, 0, 0.2, 0, 0.5, 0.5),
          direction = c("greater", "two.sided", "greater",
          "two.sided", "greater", "greater"))
#> Prior-odds threshold for directional claims
#>   m = 6, pi0 = 0.6
#>   c = 0.975, c* = 0.9832
#> 
#>    median.est null.value     pd pd.adj direction
#> H1     0.9860        0.2 0.7820 0.7051   greater
#> H2    -0.1175        0.0 0.5350 0.4341 two.sided
#> H3     0.7761        0.2 0.7230 0.6350   greater
#> H4    -0.0089        0.0 0.5030 0.4029 two.sided
#> H5     1.9500        0.5 0.9285 0.8965   greater
#> H6     2.9866        0.5 0.9948 0.9921   greater
#> 
#> pd.adj: Pr(claimed direction | y) under the prior in the class most skeptical
#>         of it; 1 - pd.adj is the probability of the other side under that prior.
#> Claim a direction when pd.adj > 0.975, or equivalently pd > 0.9832.
